lessons.title: What Is A Hash Function?
lessons.objective: Understand what a hash function does, why it enables O(1) average-case lookups, and what properties a good hash function must have.
concepts: Hash function definition: maps any key to an integer index
The modulo operation to fit index within array bounds
Determinism: same key always produces same hash
Uniform distribution: minimising collisions
Avalanche effect: small input change produces large hash change
Why lookup is O(1) average but O(n) worst case
Real hash functions: djb2, MurmurHash, FNV
lessons.explanation: A hash function takes any key — a string, an integer, an object — and converts it into an integer that serves as an index into a fixed-size array. The process is: compute hash(key), then take hash(key) % array_size to get a valid index. This single operation lets you store and retrieve values in constant time, bypassing the need to search. For a hash function to be useful it must be deterministic: the same key must always produce the same index. It must be fast to compute: ideally O(key_length), not slower. It must distribute keys uniformly across the array to minimise the chance of two keys landing on the same index (a collision). A good hash function has the avalanche effect: changing one character in a string completely changes the output hash, preventing clustering. The O(1) guarantee is an average-case claim, not a worst-case guarantee. In the worst case, if every key hashes to the same index, all operations degrade to O(n). In practice, with a good hash function and a reasonably sized array, collisions are rare and the average is effectively O(1).
lessons.analogy: A hash function is a librarian who has a specific rule for deciding which shelf any book goes on, based only on the book's title. You hand them any title and they immediately tell you the shelf number without searching. The rule must be consistent (same title always gives the same shelf), fast to apply, and must spread books evenly across shelves so no single shelf becomes overcrowded. A bad rule that puts everything on shelf 3 makes every lookup a shelf-3 search — O(n).

code_example.explanation: The multiplier 31 appears in Java's String.hashCode() and is one of the most widely used hash multipliers in production. It is prime, which reduces collision patterns, and multiplication by 31 can be optimised by compilers to a bit shift plus subtraction (31*x = 32*x - x = (x<<5) - x), making it fast even in performance-critical code.

common_mistakes: Thinking O(1) hash map lookup is guaranteed in all cases — it is an average-case claim; a poor hash function or adversarial input that forces all keys to the same bucket degrades every operation to O(n)

Using mutable objects or arrays as hash map keys in JavaScript — object identity (reference) is used for hashing by default, so two separate arrays [1,2] and [1,2] hash to different slots even though they are equal; always use primitive keys (strings, numbers) or serialise complex keys

Not understanding why the array size matters — a very small array means many collisions regardless of hash quality; most implementations automatically resize when load factor (items/capacity) exceeds ~0.75
lessons.interview_relevance: Interviewers at every level ask 'How does a hash map work internally?' The answer that earns full marks: hash function converts key to index via modulo, collisions handled by chaining or open addressing, amortized O(1) operations with occasional O(n) resize. This lesson gives you that complete answer.
lessons.mini_challenge: Implement simpleHash above and test it on these 10 keys with arraySize=10: 'a','b','c','d','e','f','g','h','i','j'. Count how many collisions occur (two keys at the same index). Then try arraySize=13 (prime) and count again. Observe that a prime array size produces fewer collisions. This is why hash table implementations use prime sizes or powers of 2 with careful handling.

lessons.title: Hash Maps — Insert, Lookup, Delete
lessons.objective: Use JavaScript's Map for all hash map operations, know the exact time complexity of each, and understand when to use Map over a plain object.
concepts: JavaScript Map: set, get, has, delete, size
Map vs plain object: key types, insertion order, prototype safety
Insert: O(1) amortized
Lookup: O(1) average
Delete: O(1) average
Iteration: O(n) in insertion order
Load factor and automatic resizing
When to use Map vs object literal
lessons.explanation: JavaScript's Map is the production hash map. Unlike plain objects, Map accepts any value as a key including functions, objects, and NaN. Map preserves insertion order on iteration. Map has a clean size property instead of requiring Object.keys(obj).length. Map has no prototype pollution risk — a plain object inherits keys like toString and constructor which can conflict with your data. Operations: map.set(key, value) inserts or updates in O(1) amortized. map.get(key) retrieves in O(1) average. map.has(key) checks existence in O(1) average. map.delete(key) removes in O(1) average. map.size returns the count in O(1). Iterating with for...of or .forEach is O(n) and visits entries in insertion order. The load factor is the ratio of stored items to total capacity. When it exceeds roughly 0.75, the map resizes to double capacity and rehashes all entries — O(n) for that one operation, O(1) amortized across all inserts. For string and number keys in non-performance-critical code, a plain object is also acceptable. Use Map when: keys are non-strings, insertion order matters, you need .size, or you are iterating frequently.
lessons.analogy: A Map is a perfectly organised filing cabinet where every drawer has a unique label (key) and contains exactly one document (value). Adding a document means making a new labelled drawer in O(1). Finding a document means reading the label directly in O(1) — no searching through drawers. Deleting means removing the labelled drawer in O(1). The cabinet automatically expands when it gets full (resize), which takes a moment but happens rarely enough that the average cost of adding a document stays O(1).

code_example.explanation: The frequency counter (freq.get(c) || 0) + 1 pattern is used in nearly every hash map problem in this module. It initialises missing keys to 0 automatically, avoiding an if-else check. This exact pattern appears in Valid Anagram, Group Anagrams, Top K Frequent Elements, and dozens of other problems.

common_mistakes: Using a plain object instead of Map and then calling .hasOwnProperty() to avoid prototype collisions — this works but is verbose; use Map from the start for any non-trivial frequency counting or key-value mapping

Reading map.get(key) without checking map.has(key) first when the value could legitimately be 0, false, or null — these are falsy, so (map.get(key) || default) would incorrectly return default; use map.has() when the value can be falsy
Iterating a Map while deleting entries — modifying a Map during for...of iteration produces unpredictable results; collect keys to delete first, then delete in a separate pass
lessons.interview_relevance: Map operations appear in virtually every hash map interview problem. The frequency counter pattern built with Map is the direct implementation of the character map technique from Module 2. Knowing Map.has() vs Map.get() semantics, insertion-order iteration, and the O(1) complexity of all core operations is baseline expected knowledge.
lessons.mini_challenge: Implement a function wordCount(sentence) that returns a Map of each word to its frequency in the sentence. Then implement a function topNWords(sentence, n) that returns the n most frequent words as an array of [word, count] pairs sorted by count descending. Use only Map — no sorting libraries. State the time complexity of your topNWords implementation.

lessons.title: Hash Sets
lessons.objective: Use JavaScript's Set for O(1) membership testing, duplicate detection, and intersection/union operations — and know precisely when Set is preferable to Map.
concepts: Set: stores unique values, no duplicates
Set operations: add, has, delete, size
O(1) average for add, has, delete
Set vs Array for membership testing: O(1) vs O(n)
Converting between Set and Array
Set intersection, union, difference
Seen-set pattern for duplicate detection
When to use Set vs Map
lessons.explanation: A Set stores unique values with no duplicates and no associated value per entry. Like Map, it uses a hash table internally, giving O(1) average for add, has, and delete. The critical advantage over Array: arr.includes(x) is O(n) because it scans linearly, while set.has(x) is O(1) because it hashes. This single difference changes the complexity of duplicate detection from O(n²) to O(n). The seen-set pattern: iterate once, for each element check set.has(element) — if true, it is a duplicate; if false, add it to the set. This is O(n) total with O(n) space. Use Set when you need: fast existence checking, deduplication, set operations (intersection, union, difference). Use Map when you need: a value associated with each key, frequency counts, or any key-to-value mapping.
lessons.analogy: A Set is a bouncer's list. Adding a name means writing it once — if it is already on the list, nothing changes. Checking if someone is on the list means one O(1) lookup, not reading every name from the top. An Array is a queue: to check if someone is in a queue, you walk from the front to the back — O(n). The bouncer's list lets you answer 'is this person here?' instantly regardless of how many people are on it.

code_example.explanation: Intersection uses filter + b.has(x). The filter is O(a.size), and each b.has() is O(1), so intersection is O(a.size) total. This is far better than the O(a*b) brute-force nested loop. This intersection pattern appears directly in LeetCode #349 Intersection of Two Arrays.

common_mistakes: Using arr.includes() inside a loop when a Set would give O(1) — this is one of the most common hidden O(n²) patterns in beginner code; any time you search an array inside a loop, ask whether a Set would work

Assuming Set preserves insertion order for iteration — JavaScript's Set does preserve insertion order, but relying on this in algorithms is a design smell; if order matters, use an array alongside the Set

Forgetting that Set equality is by reference for objects — new Set([{a:1},{a:1}]).size is 2, not 1, because the two objects are different references; always use primitive values in Sets for deduplication
lessons.interview_relevance: Set is the data structure behind O(n) solutions to Contains Duplicate (#217), Longest Consecutive Sequence (#128), and Two Sum. The pattern 'build a Set from the input, then query it in O(1)' is one of the most frequently applied transformations in all of Blind 75. Recognising when to replace an array with a Set is a fundamental interview skill.
lessons.mini_challenge: Solve Longest Consecutive Sequence (LeetCode #128): given an unsorted array of integers, return the length of the longest consecutive sequence. The brute force is O(n²) or O(n log n) with sorting. Solve it in O(n) using a Set. Hint: for each number n, only start counting a sequence if n-1 is NOT in the Set — this ensures you only count from the start of each sequence. Apply the 5-step framework before coding.

lessons.title: Collision Handling — Chaining And Open Addressing
lessons.objective: Explain how hash maps handle two keys landing on the same index, and understand why this knowledge affects how you reason about worst-case complexity in interviews.
concepts: Collision definition: two keys hash to the same index
Separate chaining: each bucket holds a linked list
Open addressing: probe for next empty slot
Linear probing and clustering problem
Quadratic probing and double hashing
Load factor: items / capacity
Resize threshold and rehashing cost
Why worst case is O(n) and when it matters
lessons.explanation: A collision occurs when two different keys produce the same array index after hashing. Collisions are inevitable for any hash table that stores more keys than it has slots — by the pigeonhole principle. Two main strategies handle them. Separate chaining: each slot holds a linked list (or dynamic array). Colliding keys are appended to that slot's list. Lookup requires hashing to the slot, then scanning the list — O(1) average when chains are short, O(n) worst case if all keys collide. Open addressing: all entries live in the array itself with no external lists. On collision, probe for the next empty slot using a probing sequence. Linear probing checks slot+1, slot+2, slot+3 — simple but causes primary clustering where long runs of filled slots form, slowing future lookups. Quadratic probing uses slot+1², slot+2² — reduces clustering. Double hashing uses a second hash function to compute the probe step — best distribution but more complex. Load factor controls performance: both strategies degrade as the table fills up. JavaScript's Map uses a combination strategy tuned per engine (V8 uses open addressing with quadratic probing). Maps automatically resize when load factor exceeds roughly 0.75, rehashing all entries into the new larger array at O(n) cost.
lessons.analogy: Separate chaining is like a hotel where each room number can hold multiple guests by adding beds. A collision means two guests get the same room — the hotel just adds a bed. Finding a specific guest means going to their room number and checking each bed. Open addressing is a hotel with exactly one bed per room. A collision means the guest walks down the corridor until they find an empty room. Primary clustering is a long corridor stretch where every room is occupied, forcing guests to walk far.

code_example.explanation: The chaining implementation shows exactly what happens when two keys hash to the same bucket — they coexist in the same array via a linear scan. This is why the average chain length equals load factor, and why keeping load factor below 0.75 is critical to maintaining O(1) average lookups.

common_mistakes: Treating O(1) hash map complexity as an absolute guarantee in all scenarios — adversarial inputs that force all keys to one bucket are a real attack vector (hash flooding); production systems use randomised hash seeds to prevent this

Not knowing the difference between chaining and open addressing when asked in interviews — being able to describe both and state their tradeoffs (chaining handles high load gracefully, open addressing has better cache locality) is a common senior interview question
Ignoring the cost of resize — when a map rehashes, every existing entry is recomputed and moved; in latency-sensitive systems this O(n) spike can be a problem even though the amortized cost is O(1)
lessons.interview_relevance: System design and senior engineering interviews explicitly ask 'How does a hash map handle collisions?' and 'What is the worst-case complexity of a hash map and when does it occur?'. Being able to describe both strategies, explain load factor, and discuss hash flooding attacks demonstrates depth beyond basic usage.
lessons.mini_challenge: Implement HashMapChaining above, then add a resize() method that doubles the bucket count and rehashes all existing entries when load factor exceeds 0.75. Test it by inserting 8 items into a size-10 map and verifying that after the 8th insert the map resizes to 20 buckets and all 8 items are still retrievable. State the time complexity of your resize operation.

lessons.title: Two Sum And Variants
lessons.objective: Solve Two Sum and its four main variants using a hash map, and generalise the single-pass complement-lookup pattern to any pair-finding problem.
concepts: Two Sum: complement lookup in a single pass
Two Sum II: sorted array — two pointers vs hash map tradeoff
Three Sum: sort + two pointers + deduplication
Four Sum: generalisation pattern
Two Sum — count pairs: frequency map variant
The complement pattern: target - current
Why hash map beats sorting for unsorted input
Deduplication with sets in k-sum problems
lessons.explanation: Two Sum is the canonical hash map problem and the most common entry-level interview question. The naive approach checks every pair: O(n²). The hash map approach: iterate once, for each element compute complement = target - current. Check if complement is already in the map. If yes, return the current index and the complement's stored index. If no, store current value and index in the map. This single pass is O(n) time and O(n) space. The insight is: instead of asking 'does any previous element pair with me?', we ask 'have I already seen the element that would pair with me?'. Three Sum extends this: sort the array in O(n log n), then for each element use two pointers on the remaining sorted subarray to find pairs summing to the negative of that element. Deduplication (skipping repeated elements at each pointer) prevents counting the same triplet multiple times. Three Sum is O(n²) time O(1) space. Understanding these variants trains the generalisation muscle: any k-sum reduces to a (k-2)-sum with two outer loops.
lessons.analogy: Two Sum with a hash map is like finding two puzzle pieces that fit together. Instead of picking up every piece and trying it against every other piece (O(n²)), you describe the shape you need (the complement) and check a lookup box of shapes you have already seen (the hash map). If the shape is in the box, you found your pair instantly. If not, you add your current piece to the box and continue. You only walk through the pile once.

code_example.explanation: Three Sum's deduplication logic (skip when nums[i] === nums[i-1]) is critical and the most common place to introduce bugs. The skip must check i > 0 first to avoid out-of-bounds access at i=0. Without deduplication, [-1,-1,0,1] would produce [[-1,0,1],[-1,0,1]] — the same triplet twice. This deduplication pattern appears in almost all k-sum problems.

common_mistakes: Storing the value without the index in the Two Sum map — the problem asks for indices, so the map must store value -> index, not value -> boolean
Not handling duplicates in Three Sum — failing to skip repeated values for the outer loop and both pointers produces duplicate triplets in the result, which is a wrong answer

Reaching for a hash map on Two Sum II (sorted input) — when the array is already sorted, two pointers gives O(n) time and O(1) space, which is strictly better than a hash map's O(n) space; always check if the input has structure that enables a better approach
lessons.interview_relevance: Two Sum (#1) is the most solved LeetCode problem and appears in virtually every junior interview. Three Sum (#15) is Blind 75 and consistently appears at mid-level interviews. Being able to solve both fluently, explain the hash map vs two-pointer tradeoff for the sorted variant, and handle duplicates in Three Sum is a clear competency signal.
lessons.mini_challenge: Solve Four Sum (LeetCode #18): given an array and a target, return all unique quadruplets that sum to target. Generalise the Three Sum approach by adding one more outer loop and applying the same deduplication logic at every level. State the time complexity. Then answer: could you solve Four Sum using a hash map instead of sorting? What would the time and space complexity be?

lessons.title: Group Anagrams Pattern
lessons.objective: Solve Group Anagrams and all fingerprinting problems by using a hash map with a computed key that captures the essential identity of each item.
concepts: Fingerprinting: a canonical key that identifies a group
Sorted string as anagram fingerprint
Character frequency tuple as fingerprint: O(n) vs O(n log n)
Map of fingerprint -> list of matching items
Generalising fingerprinting to non-anagram grouping problems
Why the key must be immutable and comparable
Trade-off: sorted key vs frequency key
lessons.explanation: Group Anagrams requires placing strings that are anagrams of each other into the same group. The key insight is fingerprinting: compute a canonical representation (fingerprint) of each string that is identical for all its anagrams. Two fingerprint strategies: sorted string ('eat'.split('').sort().join('') = 'aet', as does 'tea' and 'ate') — O(k log k) per string where k is the string length, total O(n*k log k). Frequency tuple: count occurrences of each of 26 letters and join as a string like '1_0_0_0_1_0_..._1_0_0_0' — O(k) per string, total O(n*k), better for long strings. Once you have the fingerprint, use it as a Map key and append the original string to the corresponding array. After processing all strings, return Map.values(). The fingerprinting pattern generalises beyond anagrams: any problem asking you to group items that share a property can be solved by computing a canonical key that represents that property.
lessons.analogy: Fingerprinting is like sorting the letters in a name to create a filing key. 'Tom Marvolo Riddle' and 'I am Lord Voldemort' share the same sorted-letter fingerprint. Any two strings that are anagrams of each other will always produce the same fingerprint regardless of how they are written. The filing cabinet (Map) uses the fingerprint as the drawer label and stores all strings with that fingerprint in the same drawer.

code_example.explanation: The '#' separator in the frequency key prevents false collisions that would occur if counts were simply concatenated. For example count [1,2] would join as '12' and count [12] would also join as '12' without a separator. Using a unique separator character guarantees that different frequency vectors produce different keys.

common_mistakes: Joining the frequency array without a separator — '12' could represent count [1,2] or count [12,0,...]; always use a separator character like '#' to make each frequency value unambiguous in the key string

Using a sorted array reference as the Map key instead of joining it to a string — Map equality for arrays uses reference equality, so two separate [1,2] arrays are not equal as keys; always convert to a string primitive before using as a Map key

Over-engineering the fingerprint — sorted string is perfectly correct for strings up to a few hundred characters; only switch to frequency key when profiling shows sorting is a bottleneck on very long strings
lessons.interview_relevance: Group Anagrams (#49) is Blind 75. The fingerprinting pattern directly extends to Valid Anagram (#242), Find All Anagrams in a String (#438), and beyond. Interviewers specifically ask the follow-up 'can you do better than O(n*k log k)?' — the frequency key approach is the answer.
lessons.mini_challenge: Extend groupAnagrams_freq to handle strings containing uppercase letters and digits, not just lowercase letters. The frequency array must cover all alphanumeric characters (a-z, A-Z, 0-9 = 62 characters). Rewrite the key generation and test on ['Hello','olleH','HELLO','world','dlrow']. Then implement a groupByFirstAndLastChar function that groups strings sharing the same first and last character — use fingerprinting with a simple key like firstChar + '#' + lastChar.

lessons.title: Top K Frequent Elements
lessons.objective: Find the k most frequent elements in O(n) using bucket sort — and understand why this beats the O(n log n) heap or sorting approach for this specific problem.
concepts: Frequency map: O(n) build
Naive approach: sort by frequency O(n log n)
Heap approach: min-heap of size k O(n log k)
Bucket sort approach: O(n) using frequency as index
Bucket sort insight: max frequency is bounded by n
Collecting results from buckets in reverse order
When O(n) bucket sort beats O(n log k) heap
Top K pattern generalisation
lessons.explanation: Top K Frequent Elements asks: given an array, return the k elements that appear most often. Three approaches with different complexities. Naive sort: build frequency map O(n), sort all unique elements by frequency O(m log m) where m is unique element count, take first k. Total: O(n log n). Min-heap of size k: build frequency map O(n), maintain a heap of the k most frequent elements seen so far O(n log k). Total: O(n log k) — better than sorting when k << n. Bucket sort: the maximum possible frequency of any element is n (if all elements are the same). Create an array of n+1 buckets where bucket[i] holds all elements with frequency i. Build frequency map O(n), fill buckets O(n), collect from bucket[n] down to bucket[1] taking elements until k are collected O(n). Total: O(n) — linear. The bucket sort approach works because the frequency domain is bounded: frequencies range from 1 to n, so we can use frequency as an array index. This bounded-domain insight is what enables O(n) over O(n log n).
lessons.analogy: Bucket sort by frequency is like sorting students into rows by their exam score, when scores can only be 0 to 100. Instead of comparing every student to every other student (O(n log n)), you place each student directly into row number equal to their score (O(1) per student). To find the top k scorers, start from row 100 and walk down, collecting students until you have k. You never compared two students — you just placed and collected.

code_example.explanation: The key insight: buckets array has index = frequency, value = list of elements with that frequency. Since no element can appear more than n times, the index range [0..n] is bounded. This bounded range is what makes O(n) bucket sort possible here. Contrast with general sorting where keys are unbounded and O(n log n) is the best comparison-based sort.

common_mistakes: Using the sort approach and calling it O(n log n) without recognising the O(n) bucket sort exists — in interviews, always ask yourself 'is there a bounded domain I can exploit?' before reaching for sort
Creating buckets of size n instead of n+1 — if any element appears n times (all same value), it needs bucket index n; an array of size n only has indices 0..n-1 and index n would be out of bounds

Not handling the case where multiple elements share the same frequency in the top-k results — the bucket approach naturally handles this: all elements in buckets[i] have equal frequency and are added together
lessons.interview_relevance: Top K Frequent Elements (#347) is Blind 75. The follow-up 'can you do it in O(n)?' is almost always asked when a candidate produces the O(n log n) sort solution. Knowing the bucket sort approach and being able to explain why the bounded frequency domain enables it is a strong differentiator. The O(n log k) heap approach is also acceptable and should be in your toolkit for when k is very small.
lessons.mini_challenge: Solve Top K Frequent Words (LeetCode #692): given a list of strings and k, return the k most frequent strings. Ties broken alphabetically (earlier letter wins). The bucket sort approach works but requires an additional sort within each bucket to handle alphabetical tiebreaking. Implement this and state the final time complexity. Why is it no longer purely O(n) and what is the actual complexity?

lessons.title: Encode And Decode Strings
lessons.objective: Design a stateless encode/decode system for a list of strings — understanding delimiter escaping, length-prefix encoding, and why naive approaches fail on edge cases.
concepts: Problem: serialise a list of strings to one string and back
Naive delimiter approach and why it fails on strings containing the delimiter
Length-prefix encoding: prepend each string's length
Chunked transfer encoding concept
Delimiter escaping as an alternative
Edge cases: empty strings, strings containing any character
Why this problem tests protocol design thinking
Real-world connection: HTTP chunked transfer, protocol buffers
lessons.explanation: Encode and Decode Strings is a design problem, not a pattern-matching problem. The task: write encode(strs) that converts ['hello','world'] to a single string, and decode(s) that converts it back to ['hello','world']. Naive approach: join with a delimiter like '#'. Fails when a string contains '#'. Fix: escape '#' as '\#'. But then you need to escape '\' as '\\' too, and the logic becomes complex. Better approach: length-prefix encoding. Each string is encoded as its length, a separator character, then the string content. '#4#hello#5#world' where 4 and 5 are lengths. Decode reads the length, advances past the separator, slices exactly length characters, and repeats. This works for any string content because the length tells you exactly how many characters to consume — no delimiter searching needed. Edge cases: empty string encodes as '0#', a string containing '#' encodes as '5#hel#o' and decodes correctly because the length 5 tells us to consume exactly 5 characters including the '#'.
lessons.analogy: Length-prefix encoding is like shipping packages with a label saying exactly how many items are inside before you open the box. You do not need to search for a separator between items — you read the label (length), count out exactly that many items, and whatever is in between is always the correct content regardless of what those items look like. A delimiter-based approach is like searching for the gap between packages on a conveyor belt — it fails when two packages are touching.

code_example.explanation: The inner while loop (scan to find '#') is safe because the length is always a non-negative integer, so '#' will always appear before hitting any actual string content. The outer loop terminates because i advances by at least 2 on each iteration (minimum: length '0' + '#' + '' = 2 characters consumed).

common_mistakes: Using a fixed delimiter without length-prefix encoding — any delimiter character can appear in string content; length-prefix is the only approach that handles arbitrary string content without escaping

Using split('#') in the decoder when the encoder uses length-prefix — split('#') would split on every '#' including those inside strings; always parse length-prefix by reading the length value and slicing exactly that many characters

Not testing edge cases: empty array, empty string in array, strings containing only the separator character — these three edge cases break most naive implementations and should be the first tests written
lessons.interview_relevance: Encode and Decode Strings (#271, LeetCode Premium / NeetCode 150) tests protocol design thinking, not pattern matching. Interviewers use it to assess whether you think through edge cases before coding. The problem is solvable in minutes once you know length-prefix encoding, but candidates who go straight to delimiter splitting always hit the '#' edge case and have to redesign mid-interview.
lessons.mini_challenge: Implement encode and decode above, then test all three edge cases: empty array, array containing an empty string, and array containing strings with '#' and '##'. Then answer: if string lengths could be very large (up to 10^9), would the number prefix '#' still work? What if a length itself contained '#'? Modify the encoder to use a fixed 4-byte big-endian integer prefix instead of a variable-length number string to eliminate this potential ambiguity.

lessons.title: Valid Sudoku
lessons.objective: Validate a 9x9 Sudoku board in O(1) time and space using hash sets indexed by row, column, and 3x3 box — applying the seen-set pattern across multiple dimensions simultaneously.
concepts: Sudoku validation rules: rows, columns, 3x3 boxes
Three independent seen-sets: one per row, column, box
Box index formula: (row/3)*3 + (col/3)
Composite key pattern: row-value, col-value, box-value
Single-pass O(81) = O(1) validation
Ignoring empty cells ('.')
Why not solving Sudoku — only validating
Generalising multi-constraint seen-set pattern
lessons.explanation: Sudoku validation requires checking that no digit 1-9 appears twice in any row, any column, or any 3x3 box. The brute force checks each row separately, each column separately, and each box separately — three passes of O(81) each = O(1) but with a large constant and messy code. The clean approach: one pass over all 81 cells, maintaining three arrays of Sets — rows[9], cols[9], boxes[9]. For each cell containing a digit d at position (r, c): the box index is Math.floor(r/3)*3 + Math.floor(c/3), giving 0-8 for the nine 3x3 boxes. Check if d is already in rows[r], cols[c], or boxes[boxIdx]. If any set already contains d, the board is invalid. Otherwise add d to all three. An alternative using one Set with composite string keys: a single Set storing entries like '5 in row 2', '5 in col 7', '5 in box 4'. If any entry is already in the Set when we try to add it, we found a duplicate.
lessons.analogy: Validating Sudoku with three seen-sets is like having three separate attendance registers: one per row, one per column, one per box. When a student (digit) sits down, they sign all three registers. If their name is already in any register for their row, column, or box, they are a duplicate and the board is invalid. One walk through all 81 seats, three register checks per seat.

code_example.explanation: Both implementations are O(1) time and space because the board is always 9x9 — the input size never grows. The box index formula Math.floor(r/3)*3 + Math.floor(c/3) is the key — memorise it. Integer division by 3 groups rows into [0,1,2], [3,4,5], [6,7,8] and similarly for columns, giving the 9 unique box indices 0-8.

common_mistakes: Calculating the wrong box index — the correct formula is Math.floor(r/3)*3 + Math.floor(c/3); a common error is Math.floor(r/3) + Math.floor(c/3) which gives wrong box numbers for columns 3-8
Forgetting to skip empty cells — board cells containing '.' must be ignored; adding '.' to a Set and then finding it again would incorrectly report an invalid board
Checking rows and columns but forgetting the 3x3 box constraint — the box check is the hardest to implement and the most likely to be omitted; always verify all three constraints are checked
lessons.interview_relevance: Valid Sudoku (#36) is NeetCode 150. It tests the multi-constraint seen-set pattern that appears in board validation problems generally. The box index formula is a favourite interviewer follow-up: 'How do you map a cell to its 3x3 box?' Being able to derive Math.floor(r/3)*3 + Math.floor(c/3) on the spot without hesitation is expected.
lessons.mini_challenge: Given a valid Sudoku board, implement a solveSudoku function that fills in the empty cells using backtracking. This is LeetCode #37 and a preview of the Backtracking module (L2-M04). Do not attempt to solve it optimally — write the brute-force: for each '.' cell, try digits 1-9, check validity with your isValidSudoku logic, recurse, and backtrack if no digit works. This exercise connects hash set validation with recursive search.

lessons.title: Hash Map Problem Thinking
lessons.objective: Given any new problem, identify within 60 seconds whether a hash map or hash set is the right data structure — and know exactly which hash map sub-pattern to apply.
concepts: The four hash map sub-patterns: frequency counter, complement lookup, seen set, fingerprinting
Recognition signals for each sub-pattern
Hash map as the first tool to consider for O(n²) -> O(n) reduction
When hash map does NOT help: sorted order needed, spatial locality needed
Common hash map traps: mutable keys, off-by-one in counts
Module 3 Blind 75 problems and their sub-patterns
Building the hash map reflex
skills_unlocked after this module: Hash Maps, Hash Sets
lessons.explanation: After this module you have four distinct hash map sub-patterns. Frequency counter: build a Map of element to count. Triggers: 'k most frequent', 'count occurrences', 'anagram check', 'character frequency'. Complement lookup: for each element store it and check if its complement (target - current) was seen. Triggers: 'pair summing to target', 'two sum', 'find matching element'. Seen set: use a Set to track visited elements. Triggers: 'duplicate detection', 'cycle detection', 'has element been processed', 'contains duplicate'. Fingerprinting: compute a canonical key and group by it. Triggers: 'group by equivalence class', 'anagram grouping', 'elements sharing a property'. The hash map reflex: whenever you see a nested loop that checks one array against another, or repeated linear scans, ask 'can I precompute a hash map from the first array and then answer all queries in O(1)?' This question, applied consistently, reduces most O(n²) algorithms to O(n).
lessons.analogy: The four sub-patterns are like four specialised tools in a toolbox. Frequency counter is a tally counter — press it for each occurrence. Complement lookup is a wanted poster — post what you are looking for and check if anyone matches. Seen set is a visitor log — record everyone who passed through. Fingerprinting is a filing system — file each item under its canonical identity. Recognising which tool the problem needs is the skill. Using a tally counter when you need a visitor log produces a correct but suboptimal solution.

code_example.explanation: Seven of the nine problems in this module are directly from Blind 75 or NeetCode 150. common_mistakes: Reaching for a hash map on every problem regardless of fit — hash maps give O(n) time but O(n) space; if the problem requires O(1) space and the input is sorted, two pointers is the correct tool and a hash map is wasteful

Confusing which sub-pattern to use — complement lookup and seen set both use a Set/Map but answer different questions; complement lookup asks 'have I seen target-current?' while seen set asks 'have I seen current before?'; applying the wrong one produces incorrect answers

Not practising the problems — reading this lesson and understanding the sub-patterns is preparation; the actual skill is built by opening LeetCode, solving all nine problems listed, failing, debugging, and re-solving three days later
